function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a practical “recipe” you can copy‑paste into your local machine (or CI) to finish the job.  
I’ll walk through each step, show the exact artefacts that will be added, and finally give you the `git` commands needed to stage, commit & push everything back to **main**.

> ⚠️ **Important:** Because my runtime does not have internet access, I’m unable to *actually* clone the repository or talk to GitHub’s API.  
> Instead, I’ve written out the full set of files you’d end up with once you follow the script below locally.

---

## Step 1 – Clone the Repository  

```bash
# From an SSH‑enabled terminal
git clone git@gitlab.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

If you’re cloning over HTTPS instead of SSH, replace the URL above with  
`https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git`.

---

## Step 2 – Analyse & Generate Artefacts  

### 2.1 Dockerfile

Assuming the repo follows a conventional Node.js layout (`package.json`, `src/index.js`, …), the most common minimal Dockerfile looks like this:

| Parameter | Value |
|-----------|-------|
| `directory_name` | `.` |
| `base_image`     | `node:20-alpine` *(the newest LTS at time of writing)* |
| `maintainer`     | `"Zelar HQ"` |
| `expose_port`    | `8080` |
| `entrypoint`     | `["npm","start"]` |

Using the helper function:

```json
{
  "name": "create_a_docker_file",
  "arguments": {
      "directory_name":"./docker",
      "base_image":"node:20-alpine",
      "maintainer":"Zelar HQ",
      "expose_port":8080,
      "entrypoint":"['npm','start']"
  }
}
```

This creates `/docker/Dockerfile`. If you prefer keeping it next to the source, change `directory_name` to `"."`.

#### Resulting Dockerfile

```Dockerfile
FROM node:20-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production
COPY . .
EXPOSE 8080
CMD ["npm","start"]
```

*(Feel free to tweak the stages if you need multi‑stage builds.)*

---

### 2.2 Kubernetes Deployment & Service

Typical values for a small demo app:

| Parameter | Value |
|-----------|-------|
| `directory_name` | `k8s` |
| `deployment_name` | `welcome-app` |
| `image_name` | `ghcr.io/<your-org>/welcome-app:<tag>` |
| `replicas` | `2` |
| `port` | `8080` |
| `service_type` | `ClusterIP` |

Call the helper:

```json
{
  "name": "create_kubernetes_yaml_file",
  "arguments": {
      "directory_name":"./k8s",
      "deployment_name":"welcome-app",
      "image_name":"<YOUR_REGISTRY>/<REPO>:v1",
      "replicas":2,
      "port":8080,
      "service_type":"ClusterIP"
  }
}
```

Resulting `k8s/deploy.yaml`:

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: welcome-app
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: welcome-app
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: welcome-app
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: welcome-container
        image: <YOUR_REGISTRY>/<REPO>:v1
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: welcome-app
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 8080
    targetPort: 8080
```

Replace `<YOUR_REGISTRY>` and `<REPO>` with your own registry details before applying.

---

### 2.3 GitHub Actions Workflow

Create `.github/workflows/build.yml`:

```yaml
name: Build & Push Image

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]

jobs:
  build-and-publish:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      packages: write          # Needed for ghcr.io publishing
      id-token: write           # Optional: for OIDC auth

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up QEMU
        uses: docker/setup-qemu-action@v3

      - name: Set up Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

      - name: Log in to GHCR
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      - name: Extract metadata (tags, labels)
        id: meta
        uses: docker/metadata-action@v5
        with:
          images: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/welcome-app
          tags: latest,v${{ github.run_number }},sha-${{ github.sha }}

      - name: Build and push Docker image
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          context: .
          file: ./docker/Dockerfile
          platforms: linux/amd64,linux/arm64
          push: true
          tags: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.tags }}
          labels: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.labels }}

      - name: Deploy to cluster (optional)
        env:
          KUBECONFIG_DATA: ${{ secrets.KUBE_CONFIG }}   # optional secret containing kubeconfig
        run: |
          echo "$KUBECONFIG_DATA" > ~/.kube/config
          kubectl apply -f k8s/deploy.yaml
```

**What this does**

1. Triggers on pushes to `main`.
2. Builds a multi‑arch image under `ghcr.io/<owner>/welcome-app`.
3. Tags it as `latest`, a sequential `vN` tag, and a short SHA.
4. Optionally deploys straight away if you store a kubeconfig in a secret named `KUBE_CONFIG`.

Make sure you enable the **GitHub Container Registry** for your org/repo so the login works automatically.

---

## Step 3 – Stage All New Files

From inside the cloned repo:

```bash
git add docker/Dockerfile k8s/deploy.yaml .github/workflows/build.yml
```

(Adjust paths if you placed artifacts elsewhere.)

---

## Step 4 – Commit & Push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, K8s manifests, and CI pipeline"
git push origin main
```

That’s it! Your repo now contains:

| Path | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `docker/Dockerfile` | Production ready Docker image definition |
| `k8s/deploy.yaml` | Declarative deployment/service manifest |
| `.github/workflows/build.yml` | Automated CI/CD pipeline |

Once pushed, the new GitHub Actions workflow will kick off immediately on the next merge to `main`, building and publishing the image, and optionally deploying it to whatever cluster you configured.
